purpose: This tool lets you build fractals and measure their dimension by counting copies. You see why a shape can have a dimension like 1.26, and how a random game can draw a triangle with holes.

stops.title: The figure changes by shape
stops.text: The figure changes with each shape. Shape 1 cuts a line, square and cube into copies, one in yellow. Later shapes show the Koch curve, the Sierpinski triangle, and chaos game dots. Click corners when asked to choose.
stops.try: Answer the prediction first. The copy counts for the line, square and cube appear.

stops.title: Five shapes
stops.text: 1 counts copies when you scale. 2 builds the Koch curve. 3 removes middle triangles. 4 is the chaos game. 5 lets you pick the number of copies and the scale, then shows the dimension. Each begins with a prediction.
stops.try: Choose 4, predict the shape, then press Play (4000 dots).

stops.title: Scale factor
stops.text: How many times longer each side becomes. Copies needed follow N = s to the power d, where d is the dimension: 1 for a line, 2 for a square, 3 for a cube. It stays locked until you answer the prediction.
stops.try: After predicting, set s to 5 and check the three counts.

stops.title: What Next does
stops.text: Step 1 counts copies. Step 2 builds the Koch curve and finds its dimension. Step 3 removes triangles and links to Pascal's triangle. Step 4 is the chaos game. Make your own is only in the menu.

stops.title: Try practice problems
stops.text: Seven short problems on dimension and building fractals. Press the same button to go back to the lesson. Nothing is saved or scored.

stops.title: Quick check
stops.text: A short exit ticket with explained answers.

teacher: Ask students to predict how many copies a square needs at scale 3 before moving the slider, then ask what d would make 3 to the d equal 4 for the Koch curve. Misconception: thinking the random chaos game should make a random cloud. Project step 4.
